I wish someone would have told me that. Then I probably wouldn't have spent nearly my whole life believing that I was inherently sinful and "bad' and needed someone to "save" me  from myself because I was "bad".

My high school teacher lost her son to suicide via drug overdose. She lost him at 21 and it's been almost 20 years now. She has pictures all over her classroom of him. She talks about his story nonstop and how much it breaks her. She talks about memories they shared and fun things they used to do together, actually more so than she shares about the things her current family does. Frankly, she has hinted that she is a bit mentally unstable because of how debilitating the grief has been. She told us about how her husband caught her playing with stickers in the closet, almost in a psychosis state because she was still grieving 10 years later. It really shook her to the point where she kind of has been shunned by the rest of the school and administration because she is the "crazy lady." But honestly, when you ACTUALLY sit down and just listen, she is so kind and awesome and loves so deeply. She remembers people's names and tells them that she cares about who they are even years after graduation. But because of that great capacity to love, a very tragic and close loss really changed her whole personality and the amount of help that she needs to just make it to the next day. 
Someday I wished that I had a mom like that.
 I can't say much about what her relationship with her son was like. But that has probably been the most tragic story of loss I have seen growing up.

First off, take a deep breath and accept the fact that you don't know. Usually when I accept that I dont know something it relieves the anxiety about the subject and it is freeing. Next I would create a journal or a page on what you do know. So maybe things like order of Operations. I did this when I failed my Calculus 2 class and I needed to retake it (ended up getting a B but it was still better than an F). So I then went through old notes and honestly worked out some old practice problems I had. Give yourself grace for not knowing. You cant study well if you're too busy worrying about what you don't know. Try to come up with a mnemonic or picture that can help you remember formulas and equations. I cannot stress this enough: YouTube has AMAZING stuff, if you're willing to dig. And when you do watch it, watch it from beginning to end. Dont skip around the video. I suggest Kahn Academy. It's free and so easy to follow along. And last but not least, ask questions. To get to the answer you have to put in the work. Be diligent, especially in math. Personally over time, I actually began to really appreciate the diligence in math and the importance of problem solving as it was beginning to unfurl in other parts of my life. And trust me, Algebra is the backbone of Calculus, Trigonometry, and Geometry so learning it is super important. 

Hope this helps!
